Welcome to the meeting of the Glendale Water & Power Commission. Meetings are broadcast live on cable channel 6 (GTV6) and rebroadcast throughout the week. Call (818) 548-4013 for

Glendale Avenue 4th Floor, Glendale, CA 91206. If you have any question about matters on the agenda, or requests for assistance, please contact Catalina Lee (818) 548-2107 during regular
business hours.

MINUTES
  MEETING OF THE GLENDALE WATER & POWER COMMISSION

  COUNCIL CHAMBER, City Hall – 613 E. Broadway, 2nd Floor
  Glendale, CA 91206

  July 1, 2019
  4:00 PM

1. ROLL CALL
  Present: President Avanessian, Commissioner Kedikian, Commissioner Watson
  Absent: Commissioner Carassco Carrasco, Commissioner Lall

2. CONSENT ITEMS
  a. Approval of the June 3, 2019 Meeting Minutes
  Motion to Approve:
  Moved by: Commissioner Kedikian
  Seconded by: Commissioner Watson
  Motion Passed.

3. GWP COMMISSION/ STAFF COMMENTS
  None.

4. ACTION ITEMS
  a. Draft 2019 Integrated Resource Plan and Clean Energy RFP Update
  1. Motion Recommending City Council Approval of the Draft 2019 Integrated Resource Plan
  2. Motion Providing Recommendation to the City Council

  Presentation and Commission Discussion:

  Mr. Steve Zurn provided a summary of the Integrated Resource Plan (IRP) process and explained that the IRP is
  required, by state law, to be updated at least every 5 years. Mr. Zurn introduced Ascend Analytics and Dr. Gary Dorris,
  to make the IRP presentation.

  Dr. Dorris provided an overview of the timeline related to the IRP with the City’s original repower proposal in March
  2018, the issuance of the Clean Energy RFP in May 2018, the adoption of the Interim IRP in December 2018, the
  upcoming proposed adoption of the July 2019 IRP in July, and the proposed implementation of the IPR in 2019-2022.
  Dr. Dorris stated that the IRP’s focus is on the critical needs of the City: to keep the lights on, to be clean and
  renewable, to have community participation, to be reliable, and to be economical and keep the bills low.

  Dr. Dorris explained that Glendale is unique as it relates to energy because it is isolated in many prospects; Glendale is
  electronically islanded. As such the goal is to avoid involuntary shedding of load. Dr. Dorris explained the function of
  the Pacific DC Intertie and the ramification of its failure, as well as Glendale’s interest in the Magnolia Power Plant and
  the ramifications of Magnolia transmission’s failure, and emphasized the need to ensure that there is adequate back-up
  power.

  1
 Dr. Dorris provided a summary of the Clean Energy RFP process and stated that there were numerous portfolios to be
evaluated. The portfolios were evaluated by experts from a reliability perspective and an economical perspective. Dr.
Dorris then summarized all portfolios included in the IRP and stated that the portfolio recommended in the IRP is
Portfolio E which combines battery storage, conventional generation, imported renewable resources, as well as clean
energy and load reduction.

Commissioner Kedikian inquired whether all 75 MW were going to be available before 2022 under Portfolio E. Mr. Zurn
explained that 50 will be available initially and then 25 after 2022 due to load growth and as we retire older units.

Commissioner Watson inquired regarding solar’s reduction from 140 to 130 between the different portfolios. Dr. Dorris
explained that it is due to balancing and managing costs and economics.

Dr. Dorris further explained that the City is looking to satisfy the N-1-1 criteria. Some portfolios, such as Portfolio G and
F fall short of meeting this requirement. The portfolios which meet the N-1-1 satisfaction criteria are then evaluated
based on economics. While Portfolio E is not the most economical portfolio, it is the best compromised one – it is the
least cost - most reliable option.

Dr. Dorris explained that ICE (internal combustion engines) satisfy reliable power. The Odds are very remote that the
City will get all renewable energy through transmission lines.

Commissioner Kedikian inquired about the local reliability market and how it is tied in with generation in Portfolio E. Dr.
Dorris explained that California has created a reliability mandate to address the issue of local deficits. Glendale follows
the state mandates for energy supply.

Commissioner Kedikian inquired about battery installation under Portfolio F. Mr. Zurn stated that all 100 MW, under
Portfolio F, would be installed at the same time.

Commissioner Kedikian inquired whether GWP considered phased-installation of ICEs. Mr. Zurn explained that if the
project’s permit allows for a certain number of units (for example 2) to be installed, then that is the only number
permitted and if GWP wishes to add units, then it will be subject to new permitting by AQMD.

Commissioner Watson inquired regarding hydrogen power for ICEs and whether it is considered clean fuel. Dr. Dorris
stated that hydrogen is considered clean fuel. Commissioner Watson inquired regarding the project as to when
hydrogen power will be available. Dr. Dorris explained that it is available currently, however, it is uneconomical; in
terms of economics, Dr. Dorris expects hydrogen to be more available/used in 2045 as technology evolves.

Dr. Dorris explained that Glendale is indistinguishable from Hawaii because Glendale is isolated and vulnerable,
therefore it needs the back-up generation. This is why Portfolio E looks to be the best fit, because it allows to invest in
thermal today and wait until the cost of storage comes down.

Commissioner Watson inquired why Glendale is not a member of CAISO. Mr. Mark Young explained that it is due to
Glendale being surrounded by Los Angeles/LADWP; Glendale falls under LA’s balancing authority due to the
economics being better with LA.

Commissioner Kedikian inquired how much thermal generation Glendale needs now given that technology is evolving.
Dr. Dorris explained that Glendale will need thermal generation as back up in order to keep the lights on.

Dr. Dorris stated that Glendale has been an overachiever and has surpassed the state mandates renewable portfolio
targets. Dr. Dorris further explained the electrification of transportation – with more electric vehicles (EV) in use, there
will be a significant impact of reducing GHG in the City, but there will also be an increase in energy demand. Glendale’s
carbon footprint is expected to be a negative in 2020.

  2
 President Avanessian inquired about the comparison of the different alternatives as they related to time outages. Dr.
Dorris explained that Portfolio E expects 2.4 hours of loss of load per year, which equates to just 1 day in 10 years.
Portfolio G fails the reliability standard. Under Portfolio F, there is a 2.8 hours loss of load in 2033 – not enough local
generation to keep the lights on. Dr. Dorris also explained that a 100% clean portfolio is great until there is an intertie
outage which will result in shortfalls; additionally, there is more vulnerability due to fires.

Commissioner Kedikian inquired about the reason for the installation of battery MW in intervals. Mr. Zurn explained that
it is due to economics and that AQMD does not permit batteries; AQMD permits engines and in its permitting process
requires applicant to be precise in what is proposed to be installed. Commissioner Kedikian inquired about AQMD’s
actions if Glendale obtained a permit to install 5 ICEs but only had the funds to install 3. Mr. Zurn explained that if that
were to occur, then 3 ICEs would be Glendale’s baseline.

Commissioner Watson followed up on Commissioner Kedikian’s inquiry above, and stated that it appears that the above
incremental installation option is not feasible. Mr. Zurn explained that it is due to having the City’s needs met. The City
has a gap of 77 MW which it needs to fill, which is not a N-1-1 condition. Therefore, even with Portfolio E, the City is
taking a risk. Dr. Dorris explained that the cost of storage is high; therefore, the City needs to invest in thermal
generation and defer the investment in storage until its cost is feasible.

Commissioner Kedikian inquired about the capacity factor. Dr. Dorris explained that the capacity factor is the
percentage of time that the ICE units will be on-line. Commissioner Kedikian noted that the ICEs will be running at very
low intervals.

President Avanessian asked Dr. Dorris to elaborate on gas availability vs. reliability, citing Aliso Canyon leaks. Dr.
Dorris stated that the availability of gas is not expected to be an issue. Mr. Zurn explained that Glendale does not utilize
gas from Aliso Canyon; Glendale imports its gas from other agencies.

President Avanessian inquired about the transmission line restrictions for Glendale. Dr. Dorris explained that Glendale
has 2 major interties: the Pacific DC Intertie, whose reliability is subject to question, and the Magnolia Intertie. Mr. Zurn
explained that under Portfolio E, Glendale would not have to import more power from outside. Mr. Young explained that
Glendale has a 200 MW maximum capacity and our goal is to ramp up the renewables on the transmission lines. Mr.
Zurn explained that the 200 MW maximum capacity has been considered and is a factor in Portfolio E.

Commissioner Watson inquired regarding any potential for future transmission lines. Mr. Young explained that there is
no such potential.

Commissioner Kedikian inquired regarding monitoring and ensuring that the ICEs are in fact used only as back-up
generation, due to pollution. Dr. Dorris stated that the EPA will certainly be monitoring.

Public Comment:

1. Mr. Burt Culver – Mr. Culver referenced an article relating to GWP’s participating with LADWP to purchase solar
  power. Mr. Culver stated that GWP should have had a longer RFP period and considered additional options. Mr.
  Culver stated he has Green House Gas (GHG) emissions concerns and stated that he preferred slow-roll ICE
  engines – to be installed in increments.

2. Mr. Dan Brotman – Mr. Brotman complemented GWP’s work on the Integrated Resource Plan (IRP). Mr. Brotman
  emphasized the importance of the Glendale Environmental Coalition’s and the community’s involvement. Mr.
  Brotman addressed the following topics: fossil fuel, transmission, CAISO connection, contingency reserves. Mr.
  Brotman recommended that GWP retain a third party consultant to provide a second opinion on the IRP, or, that
  GWP proceed with the all-clean projects, but defer the gas-powered portion of the plan.

  3
 3. Mr. Glenn Webb – Mr. Webb disagreed with Glendale’s analogy to Hawaii because Hawaii is surrounded by the
  ocean and Glendale is surrounded by generation facilities. Mr. Webb addressed the following topics: N-1-1
  requirements; analysis of energy supply, a complete zero-carbon plan.

4. Ms. Monica Campagna – Ms. Campagna stated that she agreed with the previous speakers. She stated that she
  would like a phased-approach at the power plant in order to see how technology evolves.

5. Ms. Susan Wolfson – Ms. Wolfson stated that she appreciated GWP’s participation with the public. Ms. Wolfson
  stated that she took issue with GWP not considering any alternatives until the public’s pressure to do so. Ms.
  Wolfson addressed the following topics: peak time; a more comprehensive approach to environmental impacts and
  technology changes over time.

6. Mr. David Eisenberg – Ceded his time to Mr. Brotman

7. Ms. Kate Unger – Ms. Unger referenced the U.S. Secretary General comments at a climate meeting relating to
  climate change.

Further Commission discussion:

Commissioner Watson inquired whether Glendale can purchase energy from CAISO. Mr. Young explained that
Glendale does transact with CAISO, however the components are restricted; there is insufficient generation in that
basin. Mr. Young further explained that Glendale is in discussions with LA relating to a conceptual plan of utilizing LA’s
line; however, it is LA’s exclusive line to meet their SB 100 requirement. Commissioner Watson stated that based on
this information the potential for Glendale to get on LA’s plan is unlikely. Mr. Zurn explained that LA has an obligation to
its own resident/customers, therefore it is very unlikely that it will sell to Glendale; very much like Glendale has an
obligation to its residents/customers and would not sell to other entities.

Commissioner Watson addressed the public comment relating to obtaining a second opinion/review of the IRP. Mr.
Zurn explained that Glendale has a deadline to submit the IRP to the California Energy Commission (CEC) by July 29,
2019. Dr. Dorris explained that the numbers are what they are in the IRP and they are accurate.

Commissioner Kedikian acknowledged and thanked the members of the community and staff for participating in the IRP
process. Commissioner Kedikian stated that he was disappointed at the ICE permit mandate of identifying all proposed
units at the time of the permit, because with technology changing it would be good to obtain the permits, however,
decide on acting on installation later. Commissioner Kedikian suggested a recommendation to the City Council that the
IRP be adopted, however, that the City Council retain authority for further approval over the ICE installations before the
actual installation. Mr. Zurn explained that the further review process will be satisfied in the current process since the
project will undergo the issuance of the Limited Notice To Proceed (LNTP) by the City Council, which will be for the
diagnostic and permitting. Subsequently, the Environmental Impact Report (EIR) will be another opportunity for City
Council review and approval, and thereafter the Final Notice To Proceed (FNTP) will be another opportunity for
additional City Council review and approval of the project.

Commissioner Kedikian also stated that recommends that the City Council require a check mechanism whereby the ICE
units will be put in service as a last resort, an example would be an on-line program enabling the residents to see when
the ICEs are operating.

Commissioner Watson stated that he appreciates the community and staff involvement in the process as a lot has
changed over the 18 months; however, our current system is about to fail at any time, therefore, deferring is not
recommended. Commissioner Watson also stated that we have no predictions of what future technology will be; the
priorities are cost and reducing our carbon footprint. Commissioner Watson also stated that there is no reason to doubt
Ascend Analytics’ recommendation that Portfolio E is the best suited portfolio for Glendale.

  4
   Commission Action:

  Commissioner Watson made a motion that the GWP Commission recommend that the City Council approve the Draft
  2019 Integrated Resource Plan and Clean Energy RFP with the following additional recommendations: 1) that the City
  Council direct GWP to use gas powered thermal generation as a last resort once installed and operating; 2) that GWP
  explore the feasibility of a monitoring method and device for the gas powered thermal generation for the public’s
  information and benefit; and 3) that the City Council review and provide final approval prior to the actual installation of
  the gas powered thermal generation.

  Commissioner Kedikian seconded the above motion. The Motion passed by unanimous vote.

5. ORAL COMMUNICATIONS
  None

6. AGENDA FORECAST
  Mr. Zurn stated that the August GWP Commission meeting will have a robust agenda covering various water items
  including water items, legislative update and customer service update. Mr. Zurn further indicated that the September
  GWP Commission meeting will be a Special Meeting during which time GWP will make a transmission presentation and
  a wildfire mitigation presentation which will address how GWP will be impacted by legislative actions relating to wildfires
  and the steps GWP is taking to comply with the mandates.

  President Avanessian and Commissioners Kedikian and Watson had no revisions to the proposed Agenda Forecast as
  presented.

7. ADJOURNMENT
  Motion to Adjourn:
  Moved by: Commissioner Kedikian
  Seconded by: Commissioner Watson
  Motion Passed.

  The meeting was adjourned at 6:46 pm.
